meta.description: Genuine Ayn Rand: John Galt’s oath in Atlas Shrugged (1957), p. 1069 of the first edition. It is a character’s vow, and the novel prints it with em-dashes.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I swear by my life and my love of it that I will never live for the sake of another man, nor ask another man to live for mine'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Ayn Rand. It is John Galt’s oath from Atlas Shrugged (1957), spoken in his radio speech and carved above a door in the strikers’ valley.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is John Galt’s oath in Atlas Shrugged (Random House, 1957). Galt says it in his radio speech in Part Three, Chapter VII, on p. 1069 of the first edition, and it is also carved above a door in the strikers’ valley. The book’s wording is “I swear—by my life and my love of it—that…”

source.excerpt: I swear—by my life and my love of it—that I will never live for the sake of another man, nor ask another man to live for mine.
trail: Wikiquote’s Atlas Shrugged page ↗ quotes the oath in full with its em-dashes. It cites p. 1069 and credits it to John Galt (radio broadcast) in Chapter VII. The page says its numbers follow the 1957 Random House hardcover.

LitCharts ↗ says that in Part 3, Chapter 1, Dagny finds an inscription beginning “I swear by my life” above the door of a small granite building that houses Galt’s experimental motor. So the oath appears in the valley before the speech.
Wikipedia ↗ dates the book: Random House published it on October 10, 1957, and the first edition ran to 1,168 pages.
Quote Investigator’s Ayn Rand articles ↗ do not include this line. None of them investigates the oath.
source.excerptNote: The wording as Wikiquote gives it from the 1957 first edition. The popular version keeps every word and drops only the two em-dashes.

author.name: Ayn Rand
author.heading: About Ayn Rand
author.bio: Ayn Rand was born in St. Petersburg in 1905. She became an American novelist and founded the philosophy she called Objectivism. Atlas Shrugged was her fourth novel, her longest and her last, and she counted it as her masterwork in fiction. Its hero, John Galt, leads a strike of the world’s most productive people, and his oath sums up the book’s rejection of self-sacrifice.

misattribution.heading: Real, but often stripped of its context
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Ayn Rand is correct. Two things usually get lost when the line circulates on its own.

items.who: Ayn Rand, as her own personal vow
items.why: In the novel the oath belongs to John Galt. Wikiquote credits it to “John Galt (radio broadcast).” Rand wrote it, but she wrote it for a fictional character. (Wikiquote ↗)
The book sets off “by my life and my love of it” with two em-dashes. Online copies usually run the sentence together. The words are the same. (Wikiquote ↗)

misattribution.truthLine: Ayn Rand wrote it as John Galt’s oath in Atlas Shrugged (1957), p. 1069 of the first edition. (Wikiquote ↗)

context.heading: Why the oath matters in the novel
lead: In Atlas Shrugged, the most productive people in the world go on strike and withdraw to a hidden valley. The oath appears twice. Dagny Taggart first sees it carved above the door of the small granite building that houses Galt’s motor (LitCharts ↗). Later Galt speaks it to the whole country during his radio broadcast in Chapter VII (Wikiquote ↗).

The oath is two promises: never to sacrifice yourself for others, and never to ask others to sacrifice themselves for you. That pairing states the novel’s case against self-sacrifice as a moral duty, and it is why the line is quoted so often on its own.
